COURT OBSERVATION 27.
Before appreciating the evidence, the Court deems it fit to reproduce and discuss the relevant provisions which have been attracted in the present case as per the chargesheet:

(a) Section 279 IPC reads as hereunder:
"279. Rash driving or riding on a public way.--Whoever drives any vehicle, or rides, on any public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both."

(b) Additionally, the accused has been charged with Section 304A IPC which reads:
"304A.Causing death by negligence -Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both."
28.
It must be noted here that "rashness" for the purpose of above said sections, has been understood to mean a hasty act done without considering the possible result.
The criminality lies in running the risk of doing an act with indifference to consequences.

Criminal negligence on the other hand is the gross and culpable neglect to take proper care and precaution to guard against injury,
either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which having regard to all the FIR No.686/2016 State Vs. Sushil Page No. 14 of 21 AVIRAL by AVIRAL SHUKLA SHUKLA Date:
2024.04.12 04:53:34 +0530 circumstances out of which the charge has arisen, it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted.
Essentially, criminal negligence is the breach of duty towards others.
29. It is a settled preposition of law that rash and negligent behavior has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case.
The two are incapable of being construed or seen in isolation and must be examined in light of the attending circumstances.

30. In the present case, it has been alleged that accused Sushil was driving his Tata 407 bearing registration no. HR S5 1445 in such a rash and negligent manner that it endangered human life and personal safety of others.

More specifically, it has been alleged that the accused struck against a bicycle in such a rash and negligent manner that the death of bicycle rider / victim Rajbir Sharma was caused (not amounting to culpable homicide).
Hence, the provisions contained within Sections 279 and 304A IPC are said to have been attracted in the present case.

33. Whilst, mere high-speed is not the sole criteria for judging 'rashness and negligence', the attending circumstances must be looked into for arriving at a conclusion.

Reliance may be placed at this stage to the judgment of Hon. Supreme Court of India in the case of Ravi Kapur v. State of Rajasthan, (2012) 9 SCC 284, wherein the following was held:
"20.

sentences.text: In light of the above, now we have to examine if negligence in the case of an accident can be gathered from the attendant circumstances.
We have already held that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is equally applicable to the cases of accident and not merely to the civil jurisprudence.
Thus, these principles can equally be extended to criminal cases provided the attendant circumstances and basic facts are proved.
It may also be noticed that either the accident must be proved by proper and cogent evidence or it should be an admitted fact before this principle can be applied.
This doctrine comes to aid at a subsequent stage where it is not clear as to how and due to whose negligence the accident occurred.
The factum of accident having been established, the Court with the aid of proper evidence may take assistance of the attendant circumstances and apply the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.
The mere fact of occurrence of an accident does not necessarily imply that it must be owed to someone's negligence.

In cases where negligence is the primary cause, it may not FIR No.686/2016 State Vs. Sushil Page No. 16 of 21 AVIRAL SHUKLA SHUKLA Date:
2024.04.12 04:53:44 +0530 always be that direct evidence to prove it exists.

Elements of this doctrine may be stated as :
 The event would not have occurred but for someone's negligence.
The evidence on record rules out the possibility that actions of the victim or some third party could be the reason behind the event.
The accused was negligent and owed a duty of care towards the victim."
34. PW1 has himself stated that when the tempo had struck against the cycle, the cycle was taken 10 meters ahead.
He has clearly stated that the offending vehicle ran over the cyclist and crushed his head.

When the IO/PW6 was cross examined on the question of distance between the offending vehicle and body of the victim, he stated that the distance between the offending vehicle and the body was about 50 feet.
He also stated that the deceased was dragged by the offending vehicle for about 30 feet.
The aforesaid testimonies of both of the witnesses indicates the sheer force with which the offending vehicle had struck against the cycle of the victim.
The sheer speed of the vehicle can also be noted from the fact that the skull of the victim was crushed in the accident.
The testimonies of PW1/complainant, PW5 ASI Sonu Nain and PW6 SI Dharampal unequivocally prove that the victim's skull was crushed and he was found lying in a pool of blood.
35. Another primary evidence placed on record by the prosecution are the Mechanical Inspection Reports of the two vehicles involved in the accident.

The Mechanical Inspection Report of vehicle Neelam Cycle (victims' vehicle) is PW- FIR No.686/2016 State Vs. Sushil Page No. 17 of 21 AVIRAL SHUKLA SHUKLA Date:
2024.04.12 04:53:49 +0530 2/A.
Upon perusal of the same, it can be noted that severe fresh damages have been reported on all parts of the cycle.
The vehicle has been reported to be 'off road in major accident'.
The Mechanical Inspection Report of the accused's vehicle i.e. Tata 407 is Ex. PW-2/B.

The same indicates a 'front impact'
with damages on the front bumper and front number plate.
The vehicle of the accused has been reported to be 'on road'.
The under carriage of the vehicle was found to be with dried blood spots / marks.

The aforesaid exhibits PW-2/A and Ex.
PW-2/B
are mutually consistent.
The Mechanical Inspector deposed as PW2 and his testimony is consistent with the case of the prosecution.
36. The other aspect for consideration is whether the offending vehicle was being driven by the accused himself?
The complainant/PW1 has testified that: " Public persons gathered and made a noise and tempo stopped after some distance.
I caught hold of driver of tempo.
However, due to crowd he ran away from the spot. "
Thereafter, PW1 correctly identified the accused in open court.

Even PW3 i.e. Rabir,
owner of the offending vehicle Tata 407, has deposed that his driver Sushil was State vs Sushil on 12 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/123462941/
11 driving the vehicle in question on the day of the incident.
PW3 identified the vehicle correctly and again stated that accused Sushil was driving the same vehicle which caused the accident.
37. When PW3 was cross examined by Ld. counsel for the accused, he clarified that although the vehicle was sold by him to one Vijay, the same was still registered in his name.
PW3 admitted that he knew Sushil prior to the date when notice u/S 133, Motors Vehicles Act was issued to him.

PW6 SI Dharampal has corroborated that it was PW3 Rajbir who had confirmed that Sushil was driving the vehicle and FIR No.686/2016 State Vs. Sushil Page No. 18 of 21 AVIRAL SHUKLA SHUKLA Date:
2024.04.12 04:53:54 +0530 Rajbir only produced the accused at the police station.
It is noted that accused Sushil is the nephew (bhatija) of PW3 Rajbir.
Hence, the versions of PW1, PW3 and PW6 are consistent inter se and can be relied upon.

38. The aforesaid attending circumstances, viz. the high speed of the offending vehicle, the force of the impact, the damages caused on the victim's vehicle and the crushing of the victim's skull indicate towards rashness and negligence on the part of the accused.
It is noted that the time of the accident was around 06:00 AM i.e. early in the morning when traffic is at its minimal.
The offending vehicle was clearly behind the victim's cycle and hit it from behind.
When PW1 attempted to hold on to the accused after the accident, he fled from the scene of the accident.

It can be safely concluded that driver of the offending vehicle indeed owed a duty of care towards other vehicles / pedestrians on the road and violated that duty by driving the vehicle at such high speed and hitting it against the cycle of the victim.
This Court is of the considered view that the attending circumstances prove the factum of rashness and negligence on the part of the present accused.
Since the offending vehicle was being driven on a public way, the prosecution has successfully proved the commission of offence under Section 279 IPC against the accused.

39. Since, the aspect of 'rash and negligent driving' has already been established in the case, the Court must proceed to appreciate the remaining evidence available on record for assessing the offence under Sections 304A IPC.
The prosecution has placed on record the MLC of Rajbir bearing no. 547750 dt. 14.03.2016 i.e. Ex. A3.
A perusal of the MLC Ex. A3 reveals that Rajbir was brought to AIIMS Trauma FIR No.686/2016 State Vs. Sushil Page No. 19 of 21 AVIRAL

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It must be noted here that "rashness" for the purpose of above said sections, has been understood to mean a hasty act done without considering the possible result.
The criminality lies in running the risk of doing an act with indifference to consequences.
Criminal negligence on the other hand is the gross and culpable neglect to take proper care and precaution to guard against injury,
either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which having regard to all the FIR No.686/2016 State Vs. Sushil Page No. 14 of 21 AVIRAL by AVIRAL SHUKLA SHUKLA Date:
2024.04.12 04:53:34 +0530 circumstances out of which the charge has arisen, it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted.
Essentially, criminal negligence is the breach of duty towards others.
29. It is a settled preposition of law that rash and negligent behavior has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case.
The two are incapable of being construed or seen in isolation and must be examined in light of the attending circumstances.
30. In the present case, it has been alleged that accused Sushil was driving his Tata 407 bearing registration no. HR S5 1445 in such a rash and negligent manner that it endangered human life and personal safety of others.
More specifically, it has been alleged that the accused struck against a bicycle in such a rash and negligent manner that the death of bicycle rider / victim Rajbir Sharma was caused (not amounting to culpable homicide).
Hence, the provisions contained within Sections 279 and 304A IPC are said to have been attracted in the present case.
